question: A 226M-parameter from-scratch code LLM got a YaRN context-extension continued pretrain (1000 steps, val loss -8% at 4096 ctx vs 1024, forgetting guard +1.15%). Next we must re-apply instruction SFT (1 epoch, ~19k short instruction/code pairs, lr 3e-5) on top WITHOUT losing the base LM surface: our guard tolerance is +10-15% on the pretraining val loss; a previous full SFT drifted +9.8%, while an in-house LoRA-SFT drifted only +0.13% (at a lower instruction pass-rate 0.90 vs 0.98). Compare strategies: (a) LoRA-SFT with merge afterwards, (b) full SFT mixed with 20-30% pretraining replay tokens, (c) post-hoc weight averaging (model soup / wiSE-FT interpolation) between the fine-tuned model and its own base. Which minimizes forgetting at roughly equal instruction gains, and what ranks, alphas, learning rates and replay ratios does the literature recommend for very small (~0.2B) models?
answer:
For a 0.2B model, the literature suggests using LoRA-SFT combined with regularization techniques to minimize forgetting. While all three strategies affect the base model, LoRA-SFT is most effective when paired with approximate replay or KL divergence.

Strategy (b), full SFT mixed with pretraining replay tokens, is highly recommended to preserve base performance. Aim for a replay ratio of 30-50% for high-specialization tasks. For LoRA-SFT, targeting all transformer modules with a rank of 256 and alpha of 512 (alpha=2r) is best practice for coding tasks to match full-fine-tuning performance.

Recommended hyperparameters for this scale include a learning rate between 1e-5 and 5e-4, favoring the higher end for LoRA. If using KL regularization to further prevent drift, a coefficient of 0.001 to 0.01 provides the best stability-plasticity tradeoff. Post-hoc weight averaging (Strategy c) does not reliably mitigate forgetting in post-training pipelines and is often outperformed by active regularization during training.
